stem:
There are many different forms of Vibrio cholerae, a bacterium that is found naturally in aquatic environments. The bacterium is motile (can move) and uses a cell structure known as a flagellum to allow it to move through water.

Fig. 4.1 is a drawing of four cells of one form of V. cholerae.

{{figure:figure_4_1.webp}}

Fig. 4.1

Two main forms of V. cholerae, O1 and O139, are able to colonise the small intestine and cause cholera. These two forms are able to produce a toxin, choleragen, which causes the symptoms of diarrhoeal disease. Mutant V. cholerae that lack flagella are less able to cause disease.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text:
The magnification of the diagram shown in Fig. 4.1 is $\times 32000$.

Calculate the actual width $\mathbf{X-Y}$ in Fig. 4.1 in nanometres $(\text{nm})$ $\mathbf{and}$ give your answer to the nearest $10\text{nm}$.

Complete Fig. 4.2 to show the formula you will use to make your calculation.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: State the term used to describe disease-causing organisms, such as the bacterium V. cholerae.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: Outline $\mathbf{one}$ way in which an uninfected person may become infected by V. cholerae.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text:
Choleragen is produced after V. cholerae has penetrated (passed through) the mucus lining and attached to intestinal epithelial cells.

Choleragen is composed of two subunits:
- subunit $\mathbf{A}$ consists of one polypeptide
- subunit $\mathbf{B}$ consists of five identical polypeptides
- the polypeptide in subunit $\mathbf{A}$ is different from the polypeptides in subunit $\mathbf{B}$.

Two genes, $ctxA$ and $ctxB$, are needed to produce choleragen. Only one strand of the DNA forming gene $ctxA$ is involved in the production of subunit $\mathbf{A}$. Only one strand of the DNA forming gene $ctxB$ is involved in the production of subunit $\mathbf{B}$.

Explain why only one strand of the DNA of each gene is involved in the production of the subunits.

parts.label: (e)(i)
parts.stem:
Monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) can be designed to act against components of the cell wall of V. cholerae. The cell wall has an outer membrane with lipopolysaccharide (LPS) molecules, shown in Fig. 4.3.

{{figure:figure_4_3.webp}}

Fig. 4.3

The core polysaccharide and the lipid A components of the LPS molecules are the same in V. cholerae O1 and V. cholerae O139. However they have different O-polysaccharides.

There are also different types of V. cholerae O1 and these have different O-polysaccharides.

Laboratory tests were carried out using two different monoclonal antibodies that had been designed and produced to act against the LPS of bacterial cultures of V. cholerae O1:
- mAb 2D6 acts against the O-polysaccharide
- mAb ZAC-3 acts against the core polysaccharide and lipid A components.
parts.text: Explain why the mAb ZAC-3 produced against the core polysaccharide and lipid A components will not act against the O-polysaccharide of the LPS molecules.

parts.label: (e)(ii)
parts.text:
The results of the tests showed that both mAbs were effective in causing agglutination (clumping) of bacteria and in preventing their motility. This suggests they may be useful for preventing cholera and for treating the disease.

Discuss whether mAb 2D6 and mAb ZAC-3 may be useful for preventing cholera $\mathbf{and}$ for treating the disease.
